items.q: Complete the deck's definition: *"Procurement is the process of ______ materials from vendor, ______ it and finally ______ the vendor for the accepted materials."*
options: sourcing … inspecting … paying
planning … receiving … invoicing
ordering … storing … settling
requisitioning … valuing … reconciling
items.explain: **Sourcing · inspecting · paying.** Note the second definition the deck also gives — *"procurement management is a **strategic approach to optimizing organizational spend**"* — which is the same function described at **level 3 of the maturity model** rather than level 1.

items.q: Why is procurement called a **fundamental module** of any ERP system? *(select all that apply)*
options: It is a requirement for almost every organization
It is a transaction intensive process
It is a widely used module
It is the only module that posts to the general ledger
items.explain:
**Universal, transaction-intensive and widely used** — the classic ERP case, since high volume and rule-governed work is exactly what automation pays for.

⚠️ Option D is false: **every** module posts to the GL. That was Unit 3's point about Financial Management being the one module that receives input from all the others.

items.q: In the deck's **eight-stage procurement cycle diagram**, which stage comes immediately after **Order Processing**?
options: Purchase Order Monitoring
Goods Receipt
Vendor Selection
Invoice Verification
items.explain:
**Purchase Order Monitoring** — chasing the order after it is placed.

The full cycle: **Requirement Determination → Source of Supply Determination → Vendor Selection → Order Processing → Purchase Order Monitoring → Goods Receipt → Invoice Verification → Payment Processing.**

**Draw the eight-stage version** — every shorter version of the cycle collapses out of it.

items.q: **Three-way matching** matches the invoice against which two documents?
options: Goods Receipt and Purchase Order
Purchase Requisition and Purchase Order
Goods Receipt and Delivery Schedule
Contract and Source List
items.explain:
**GR and PO** — *"auto matching of invoices with **GR qty** and **P.O. price**."*

**Match quantity against the GR; match price against the PO.** Why three and not two: **PO + invoice agreeing proves nothing was delivered**; **GR + invoice agreeing proves nothing about the agreed price.** Only all three close both gaps.

items.q: **ERS — Evaluated Receipt Settlement** — what does it eliminate, and at which maturity level does it sit?
options: The vendor's invoice; level 2 (matured processes)
The purchase order; level 1 (basic processes)
The goods receipt; level 3 (innovative processes)
The purchase requisition; level 2 (matured processes)
items.explain:
**ERS pays from the GR and the PO alone — no invoice.** If **PO price × GR quantity** already gives the right amount, the invoice adds no information, only a document to match.

**It is level 2, not level 1**, because it is not a feature you switch on — it needs total price agreement and enough trust that neither party requires the invoice as evidence.

items.q: Distinguish a **blocked** invoice from a **parked** invoice.
options: Blocked = complete but held for a variance or inspection; parked = entered but incomplete
Blocked = entered but incomplete; parked = complete but held for approval
Blocked = rejected outright; parked = paid but not posted
They are two names for the same status
items.explain:
**Blocked = complete but disputed. Parked = incomplete.**

Blocking reasons the deck names: **quality inspection, amount variances, manual blocking/releasing.** Parking is saving an incomplete invoice without posting it.

Corrections *after* posting use **credit memos** (reduce what you owe) and **debit memos** (increase it).

items.q: What is the difference between a **quantity contract** and a **value contract**?
options: A quantity contract commits to a quantity; a value contract commits to a spend
A quantity contract is plant-specific; a value contract is central
A quantity contract covers goods; a value contract covers only services
A quantity contract is short-term; a value contract is long-term
items.explain:
**Quantity contract = *we will buy 10,000 units*. Value contract = *we will spend ₹50 lakh*.** Each is exhausted when its own measure is used up.

**Which you use depends on which side is predictable.** For **services** — where *"price comparison is complex"* and no two units are alike — **value is the only meaningful unit**.

⚠️ The **central vs plant-specific** split is a *separate* axis: who may release against the contract.

items.q: A **source list** holds suppliers in three states, material-wise. Which are they?
options: Allowed · Preferred · Blocked
Approved · Pending · Rejected
Primary · Secondary · Reserve
Active · Inactive · Archived
items.explain:
**Allowed / Preferred / Blocked**, and its purpose is **control, not convenience**.

**"Blocked" is the important state** — a vendor whose quality failed or whose certification lapsed must not be orderable, and relying on every buyer to remember that is not a control.

Note **"material wise"**: a vendor can be preferred for one material and blocked for another.

items.q: What are the three types of **delivery schedule**, and why is a delivery schedule needed?
options: Forecast, Detailed, Firm — so the supplier can plan capacity and materials properly
Weekly, Monthly, Quarterly — so orders can be consolidated
Draft, Approved, Released — so approvals can be tracked
Standard, Expedited, Emergency — so priorities are clear
items.explain:
**Forecast · Detailed · Firm** — *"for better planning by the supplier."*

**They are Unit 3's time fences published outward to the vendor.** Without them the supplier sees only firm orders arriving with your lead time and must guess about everything beyond — guessing badly means **excess stock at their end (which you pay for in the price)** or **stock-outs at yours**.

items.q: In **service procurement**, goods receipt is replaced by what?
options: Service entry and acceptance
Invoice verification
A service master record
A value contract
items.explain:
**Service entry sheet → acceptance → invoice verification.** Nothing physically arrives at a gate, so there is nothing to receive, inspect or put away.

**Acceptance is a judgement where goods receipt was a measurement** — which is exactly why service procurement is harder to control.

items.q: Which statements describe **indirect items** rather than direct items? *(select all that apply)*
options: Demand is driven by past consumption trend, not end-item demand
Planning is consumption based
Procurement can be done by the end user through E-Procurement or a Portal
Procurement department must collaborate with the supplier to design the component
items.explain:
The first three are the indirect column. **Option D is the *direct* item row** — collaboration on component design.

**This is Unit 3's dependent vs independent demand exactly:** direct = dependent = **MRP**; indirect = independent = **CBP**.

And the self-service row is a deliberate decision to stop controlling something: **a buyer's time spent negotiating a ₹500 order costs more than the order.**

items.q: **Hedging** for commodity procurement means
options: taking a position in the futures market opposite to the one in the physical market, to limit price-change risk
buying from multiple suppliers in fixed proportions to reduce supply risk
running a reverse auction to force the price down
signing a long-term fixed-price contract with one supplier
items.explain:
**Opposite position in futures.** You are going to *buy* copper, so a price **rise** hurts — take a futures position that **gains** when copper rises.

$$\textbf{physical loss} + \textbf{futures gain} \approx 0$$

**You have not made money — you have removed uncertainty.** ⚠️ Option B is a **quota arrangement**; option C is a **reverse auction**. **Auction = price discovery; hedging = price certainty.**

items.q: In the item strategy matrix, which driver belongs to **Critical Items (e.g. spares)**?
options: "Should never be out of stock"
"Price is right"
"Purchase admin cost should be low"
"Need closer collaboration with vendor"
items.explain:
**Critical items sit at high strategic impact, low financial impact** — a ₹2,000 spare whose absence stops the plant.

The other three: **Commodities** → *price is right* · **MRO** → *purchase admin cost should be low* · **Production items** → *need closer collaboration with vendor*.

**The two axes are genuinely independent** — that is why the off-diagonal quadrants exist.

items.q: Which items belong to **Level 3 (Innovative Processes)** of the procurement maturity model? *(select all that apply)*
options: Sourcing optimization
Auctions and reverse auctions
Advanced supplier analytics
E-procurement
items.explain:
**E-procurement is level 2**, not 3 — buying through a portal is automation; **running a competitive auction is a sourcing strategy.**

The three levels as relationships: **level 1 the vendor is someone you send orders to · level 2 someone you share information with · level 3 someone you build products with.** **Transact → share → co-create.**

items.q: Name the four **master data objects for ERP procurement**.
options: Material Master · Vendor Master · Terms and Conditions Master · Service Master / Service Catalog
Material Master · Customer Master · Contract Master · Pricing Master
Vendor Master · Purchase Info Record · Source List · Quota Arrangement
Material Master · BOM · Work Center · Routing
items.explain:
**What · who · on-what-terms · and the awkward fourth one.**

⚠️ Option D is the **production** master data from Unit 3 (*"My BOM Works Right"*). Option C lists procurement *functionalities*, not master data.

**The Service Master exists precisely because** *"sometimes it is difficult to define a service specification during procurement"* — specify once, reuse.

items.q: **Procurement Cycle Time** is defined as the average time between which two events?
options: Requisition submission and PO placement
PO placement and goods receipt
Requisition submission and vendor payment
Goods receipt and invoice verification
items.explain:
**Requisition → PO.** The boundary is deliberate: that is the part **procurement actually controls**. The vendor's lead time is not theirs to shorten.

**A well-chosen KPI stops at the edge of the team's authority.**

And **Procurement ROI** is the subtle companion — *"ratio of savings made by operating costs"* — because savings alone can always be increased by hiring more negotiators.

items.q: How many levels does the **inventory management pyramid** have, and what are they?
options: Three — Inventory Control · Inventory Planning · Strategic Inventory Optimization
Four — Transaction · Control · Planning · Strategic
Three — Transaction · Planning · Strategic
Five — one for each inventory model
items.explain:
**Three levels** — the question bank asks for three, and **the pyramid merges transactions and control into one base level.**

The deck's own annotation confirms it: **Transactions & Inv Control (Lose) → Inventory Planning (Maintain) → Strategic IM Processes (Gain).**

⚠️ The slide *text* elsewhere lists **four process groups** — same thing, different cut. **Three pyramid levels, four process groups.**

items.q: The pyramid levels are annotated **Lose · Maintain · Gain**. What does that mean?
options: Control done badly loses money; planning keeps you competitive; strategy is where you beat competitors
Each level loses, maintains or gains inventory value
It ranks the levels by implementation cost
It describes whether ERP support is weak, adequate or strong
items.explain:
**Accurate records are table stakes; strategy is advantage.**

- **Control = Lose** — doing it well wins nothing; doing it badly loses money to shrinkage and wrong counts
- **Planning = Maintain** — correct models keep you level with peers
- **Strategic = Gain** — VMI, CPFR, cross-docking are where you beat competitors

And the ordering is **strictly dependent upward**: you cannot run a model on figures that are wrong.

items.q: Which are the **four inventory transaction processes**? *(select all that apply)*
options: Goods Receipt
Goods Issue
Reservations
Stock Transfer
items.explain:
All four — **in · out · sideways · spoken for.**

**Reservation is the odd and interesting one:** it moves no goods at all. It changes **availability**, not **quantity** — and that distinction between physical stock and available stock is what makes an **ATP check** meaningful.

items.q: In the deck's ABC figures, **A items** account for what share of value and of items?
options: 60.5% of value, 13.3% of items
80% of value, 20% of items
60% of value, 25% of items
50% of value, 10% of items
items.explain:
**A = 60.5% of value, 13.3% of items · B = 25% / 26.7% · C = 14.5% / 60%.**

Roughly an **order of magnitude** difference in value-per-item between an A and a C — the Pareto principle measured.

⚠️ Note the criterion: **annual value of *consumption*** (consumption per period × unit price), **not unit price alone**.

items.q: Match the classification scheme to its criterion. Which pairing is **correct**?
options: HML — unit price, i.e. does not take consumption into account
ABC — source of procurement
SDE — seasonality
GOLF — issues from store
items.explain:
The full table *(from a slide with **no text layer at all**)*: **ABC** *(Always Better Control)* — usage value · **GOLF** *(Govt, ordinary, local, foreign)* — source of procurement · **SOS** *(Seasonal, off seasonal)* — seasonality · **HML** *(High, Medium, Low)* — **unit price** · **FSND** — issues from store · **SDE** *(Scarce, difficult, easy)* — procurement difficulties.

**ABC and HML are the pair most often confused** — a gold-plated bolt bought twice a year is **H under HML and C under ABC**.

items.q: Which two **stock valuation methods** does the deck name, and where does the standard price live?
options: Moving average price and standard price — the standard price is held in the Material Master
FIFO and LIFO — both held in the Vendor Master
Moving average price and replacement cost — held in the Costing view of the BOM
Standard price and net realisable value — held in the General Ledger
items.explain:
**Moving average** recalculates stock value on every receipt; **standard price** is fixed and differences post to a **variance account**.

That is exactly the Unit 3 SAP GL document: **Inventory 245.00 · Goods Received 275.00 · Price Variance 30.00** — received at 275, valued at the standard 245, **30 to variance**.

**Why you want the variance:** product cost stays comparable month to month, and purchasing performance becomes visible instead of hidden in the stock value.

items.q: The **Q model** and the **P model** are opposites. Which describes the **P model**?
options: Fixed review interval, variable order quantity
Fixed order quantity, variable timing
Fixed minimum and maximum stock levels
Order when the first of two bins empties
items.explain:
**P = periodic review: frequency constant, quantity differs.** The deck states it outright — *"opposite of Q model — qty differs, freq is constant."*

**Q fixes the quantity and lets timing float; P fixes the timing and lets quantity float.**

$$Q = M - (\textbf{stock on hand at review})$$

**The practical argument for P is consolidation** — review every item from one vendor on the same day and place **one order, one delivery**.

items.q: State the **reorder point** formula from the deck, and say what it assumes.
options: ROP = Daily Demand × Lead Time — it assumes both demand and lead time are certain
ROP = Annual Demand / Order Quantity — it assumes constant ordering cost
ROP = (Max − Min) / 2 — it assumes a symmetric consumption pattern
ROP = Annual Sales / Average Inventory — it assumes steady turnover
items.explain:
$$\textbf{ROP} = D \times LT$$

**Reorder while you still have enough stock to survive the lead time.** 50 units/day, 6-day lead time → reorder at **300**.

⚠️ It assumes **certainty**, which is why real systems add safety stock: $$\textbf{ROP} = (D \times LT) + \textbf{safety stock}$$

**Option B is the ordering-cost term of EOQ; option D is Inventory Turn.**

items.q: On the **EOQ cost curve**, why does total cost have a minimum?
options: Ordering cost falls as order quantity rises while holding cost rises — their sum has a trough
Both costs fall until a capacity limit is reached
Holding cost is fixed and ordering cost falls, so total cost falls to a floor
Demand variability creates a minimum-variance point
items.explain:
$$\textbf{Total annual cost} = \textbf{annual ordering cost} + \textbf{annual holding cost}$$

**Ordering cost** $\propto 1/Q$ — bigger lots mean fewer orders, spreading the fixed cost per order. **Holding cost** $\propto Q$ — bigger lots mean more average stock.

**One term falls, the other rises, so the sum has a minimum — the EOQ.** This is Unit 3's lot sizing with the arithmetic written down.

items.q: The **two-bin model** is described as ideal for class C items. Why?
options: It needs no system, counting or calculation — an empty bin is the reorder signal
It holds the least total inventory of any model
It gives the most accurate reorder point
It allows the largest order quantities
items.explain:
**Its genius is that it needs no system at all.** For **class C items**, running a planning calculation would cost more than the stock being planned.

**The second bin is literally the safety stock and lead-time cover.** And it is a **pull system** — consumption triggers replenishment, nobody schedules it. **Two-bin is Kanban with bins instead of cards.**

items.q: **Cross docking** eliminates which warehouse steps, and what does it cost you in exchange?
options: Put-away, storage and picking — in exchange you lose the buffer that absorbs a late truck
Goods receipt and quality inspection — in exchange you lose traceability
Picking and packing — in exchange you need more warehouse space
Goods issue and shipping — in exchange you need more vehicles
items.explain:
**Inbound dock → straight across → outbound truck.** The warehouse becomes a **sorting hub rather than a store**, and what it eliminates is not just handling but **inventory itself**.

⚠️ **The cost is slack.** It only works if inbound and outbound schedules are tightly synchronised — **one late truck stalls the flow, because there is no buffer stock.** Which is why it sits at the strategic level and needs *"channel integration with suppliers."*

items.q: **Inventory Turn** is defined as
options: Annual sales / Average inventory level
Average inventory level / Annual sales
Obsolete and scrap inventory / Gross inventory value
Volume of storage / total storage capacity
items.explain:
A turn of **12** means roughly **one month of stock on hand**; a turn of 4 means three months. **Higher is generally better** — same sales supported by less tied-up cash.

⚠️ **But not unboundedly.** Push turns up far enough and the **stock-outs** KPI starts rising. **The two are meant to be read against each other**, which is the point of measuring both.

Option C is **obsolescence**; option D is **storage space utilization**.

items.q: Distinguish **shrinkage** from **cycle counting accuracy**.
options: Shrinkage is the value actually lost; cycle counting accuracy is how well you know what you have
Shrinkage is theft only; cycle counting accuracy includes theft and damage
They measure the same thing at different frequencies
Shrinkage applies to finished goods; cycle counting accuracy applies to raw materials
items.explain:
**Shrinkage** = *costs of breakage, pilferage, deterioration.* **Cycle counting accuracy** = variance between the physical count and the perpetual record.

⚠️ **You can have low shrinkage and terrible accuracy** — nothing is being lost, but your records are a mess. **That is dangerous in its own right**, because the planning layer is running on wrong numbers. **The Lose level of the pyramid, stated as a metric.**

items.q: What level of fit does the deck say a package should achieve, and why not 100%?
options: 75–80% — no package meets 100% of a company's needs, and a package built for you would not be a package
90–95% — anything less requires unacceptable customization
50–60% — the rest is expected to be customized
100% — anything less should disqualify the package
items.explain:
**"No package will meet 100% of the company's needs. Objective is to find a package that is a good-fit (75–80% match)."**

**Why not 100%:** the economics of ERP is that **development cost is shared across thousands of customers** — which only works if the software is standard.

The three named benefits — **lower user resistance, reduced training needs, less organizational adaptation** — all follow from **less customization and less forced BPR**.

items.q: Why is package selection a **two-step** process rather than one?
options: Cheap criteria eliminate cheaply; expensive criteria are spent only on survivors
Regulators require a documented two-stage process
Vendors will not demo until they are shortlisted
The budget for evaluation is released in two tranches
items.explain:
$$\textbf{screening: many packages} \times \textbf{few criteria} \;\longrightarrow\; \textbf{selection: few packages} \times \textbf{many criteria}$$

The final evaluation compares against *"the list of requirements (**100s**)"* — running that against twenty packages is unaffordable.

**Same economics as RCCP vs CRP and ABC-driven cycle counting: match the cost of the check to the size of the remaining decision.** The shortlist is deliberately **"two to a maximum of three"** — small enough to evaluate, large enough to retain negotiating leverage.

items.q: Why are **financial viability** and **installed base** important package selection criteria?
options: Because switching ERP is prohibitively costly, so vendor survival is itself a risk you are buying
Because larger vendors always have better functionality
Because auditors require a solvency check on all IT suppliers
Because licence costs fall as installed base grows
items.explain:
The deck answers with acquisitions: **JD Edwards, PeopleSoft, Siebel, Retek → Oracle** · **Manugistics → JD Edwards** · **BAAN, Commerce One → gone.**

**You cannot change ERP the way you change a text editor** — implementation, migration, retraining and process redesign all have to be paid again. **Choosing the vendor is a lock-in decision.**

**Installed base is the evidence**, and it must be the *relevant* base — **geography specific, industry domain specific, MNC**.

items.q: **TCO** for an ERP package comprises which components?
options: Initial capital · AMC · scaling number of users
Licence cost only
Licence cost and hardware cost
Implementation cost and training cost
items.explain:
**Two of the three are recurring** — AMC forever, and every new hire is a new licence. **So a package that is cheaper today can be more expensive over ten years.**

⚠️ And the sharpest question on the deck's own evaluation list: ***"Is the customization cost included in the ERP cost?"*** Almost always **no** — which is how the cheapest package at selection becomes the most expensive by go-live.

items.q: In final package selection, requirements are categorised **Vital, Essential and Desirable**, and matches as **full, partial or none**. Why two dimensions?
options: A package matching 900 of 1,000 requirements may still be disqualified if a Vital one is a No-match
Because vendors score the two dimensions separately
Because functional and technical requirements are evaluated by different teams
Because partial matches are priced differently from full matches
items.explain:
$$\textbf{how well it matches} \times \textbf{how much that requirement matters}$$

**A one-dimensional count of matches is misleading.** *Vital* means the business cannot operate without it, so a **No-match there is disqualifying regardless of total score** — while a package missing 200 *Desirable* requirements may be the right choice.

**VED is the requirements counterpart of ABC for inventory and impact levels for risk.**

items.q: Which are stated reasons why companies **do not** follow the traditional package-selection process? *(select all that apply)*
options: Pressure from major customers to be on the same platform as them
Same ERP for all companies in the group, to solve integration / consolidation problems
Price becomes the dominant factor, especially for SMB
The board mandates an open-source solution
items.explain:
Plus a fourth the deck lists: **industry specific functionality.**

**Three of the four are perfectly rational** — a constraint outside the evaluation outweighs everything inside it. **Group standardisation is the direct answer to Unit 1's Nestlé problem** (nine general ledgers), which arose precisely because divisions chose independently.

⚠️ Reason 4 is better described as **one criterion dominating all others**, since industry experience *is* one of the criteria.

items.q: Which clause is the one companies most often omit from an ERP vendor contract and most expensive to lack?
options: License cancellation costs
Payment terms
List of deliverables along with software
Software installation help
items.explain:
**You negotiate the exit while you still have leverage** — before signing, while they still want the deal. Afterwards you have none.

The other two that hurt: **"how future upgrades will be provided *and at what cost*"** (without it, every mandatory upgrade is a negotiation you cannot walk away from), and **the vendor's implementation audits** — *final blueprint audit* and *audit before go live*, which are the **vendor checking your implementation** and which you actually want agreed in advance.

items.q: Which vendors does the deck place in **Tier 1** of the ERP package market?
options: SAP and Oracle
SAP, Oracle and Microsoft Dynamics
IBM and Accenture
Infor, IFS and Epicor
items.explain:
**Tier 1: SAP, Oracle.** **Tier 2: Microsoft Dynamics, JD Edwards, PeopleSoft, Infor, IFS, Epicor, Lawson** *(and QAD)*. **Tier 3: small and local players.**

⚠️ Option C is **Tier 1 of the *consulting* market** — IBM, Accenture, SAP.

**The tiers segment by customer size, not quality.** A Tier 1 package is frequently the *wrong* choice for a small company.

items.q: Why do **preconfigured templates** exist for the SMB segment?
options: Configuration effort is roughly fixed while its value scales with company size, so for small firms the consulting bill exceeds the licence
SMBs are legally required to use standard configurations
Templates are the only way to support multi-country statutory reporting
Vendors cannot sell licences to SMBs without them
items.explain:
$$\text{large firm: } \frac{\text{config cost}}{\text{benefit}} \text{ small} \qquad \text{small firm: } \frac{\text{config cost}}{\text{benefit}} \text{ large}$$

**The template collapses that ratio by making configuration a product rather than a project.**

**What you give up is choice** — the template embeds someone else's view of the process. **This same idea returns in Unit 5 as the enabling condition for SaaS ERP**, where customization is forbidden outright.

items.q: The deck names two ways of selecting a vendor. Which does it say ERP vendors are generally selected by?
options: Competitive bidding only
Two-phase acquisition only
Direct nomination by the steering committee
Reverse auction
items.explain:
**Competitive bidding** — *"the vendors bid and the most competitive one is awarded the contract, **provided he fulfills the requirements**."* Note the qualifier: bids clear a **technical threshold first** and compete on price second.

**Two-phase acquisition** evaluates on **actual work delivered** in a second phase — better evidence, higher price. **It is rarely used because few firms will do substantial unpaid work.**

items.q: In the RFP process, what is the purpose of the optional **RFI** step?
options: A cheap request for basic information to cut a long list down to a shortlist before full proposals are written
A formal request for the vendor's financial statements
A post-selection information pack sent to the winning bidder
A regulatory filing required for public sector procurement
items.explain:
**RFI shortlists; RFP selects** — the same two-step screening-then-selection economics as package selection.

Two other details in the process worth knowing: **release includes conference call, common meeting and media advertisement** so **every bidder hears the same clarifications** (and the process is open, not invitation-only); and **Partner Selection → Contract Negotiations → Partner Finalization → Contract Signing** are separate steps, so if negotiations fail you can still turn to the runner-up.

items.q: Where does the deck say an **in-house implementation team** may actually work?
options: Rollouts, where the first site was done by consultants and subsequent sites by the in-house team
First-time implementations at a single site
Any project where the core team is full-time
Public sector implementations
items.explain:
**Rollouts** — *"implementation in the first site had been done by the consulting team and subsequent rollout by the in-house team."* **The hard part — the blueprint — has already been paid for; site two is repetition, not design.**

⚠️ Note the deck contradicts the in-house team's own headline advantage: *"no money goes outside"* is listed as a pro, but *"overall may not work out to be cost effective **if all internal costs are factored**"* is a con. **The saving is visible; the cost is invisible.**

items.q: In the phase-wise offshoring table, which phase has the **highest** offshore percentage, and which has **0%**?
options: Support at 80%; Project Preparation at 0%
Realization at 70%; Business Blueprint at 0%
Final Preparation at 50%; Support at 0%
Business Blueprint at 90%; Realization at 0%
items.explain:
**Preparation 0% · Blueprint 10% · Realization 70% · Go Live 50% · Support 80%.**

$$\textbf{offshore \%} \;\propto\; \frac{1}{\textbf{customer contact required}}$$

**The dip at Go Live is the informative point** — it falls from 70% back to 50% because go-live needs **training, hand-holding and physical presence**.

**The general rule: work that is *specified* can be offshored; work that is *discovered* cannot.**

items.q: Which activities does the deck list as **difficult to offshore** (hence done on-site)? *(select all that apply)*
options: Business blueprinting
Integration testing and UAT
End user training and change management activities
Unit testing and volume testing
items.explain:
**Unit and volume testing are on the "commonly offshored" list** — that split is examinable.

- **Unit testing** checks *does this do what the spec says?* — self-contained
- **Integration testing** needs cross-module business judgement
- **UAT** is by definition **the business users deciding** — it cannot be offshored because **the people doing it are the customer**

*(Configuration and data migration sit in the middle — offshorable "to a limited extent".)*

items.q: How many **levers of ERP project scope** does the deck name, and what instruction accompanies them?
options: Nine — "identify in-scope and out-of-scope items clearly (and get sign off)"
Five — "agree the scope with the steering committee"
Nine — "freeze the scope before blueprinting begins"
Seven — "prioritize the scope as Vital, Essential and Desirable"
items.explain:
**Location · Business · Process · Application · Interface · Report · Data Migration · User · Technology.**

**A lever is something you can pull to make the project bigger or smaller** — which is the practical value: when over budget, **you have nine choices, not nine hundred.**

**Writing down what is *out* of scope is harder and more valuable than what is in** — because *"frequent change in scope"* is a named risk, and **an unstated exclusion is an assumed inclusion.**

items.q: Distinguish **process scope** from **application scope**.
options: Process scope is horizontal — a business process end to end; application scope is vertical — which modules are implemented
Process scope covers manufacturing; application scope covers finance
Process scope is defined by the client; application scope by the consultant
They are the same thing described at two levels of detail
items.explain:
**Procure-to-Pay runs through MM and FI** — that is process scope. ***FI, CO, MM, SD*** — that is application scope.

⚠️ **You can implement a module without implementing every process that uses it.** A project scoped as *"MM and FI"* may quietly omit **service procurement** even though both its modules are in.

**Scope by process, verify by application** — or you find the gap at integration testing.

items.q: In data migration, the transaction-data object list uses one word repeatedly. What is it, and what principle does it encode?
options: "Open" — you migrate what is unfinished, not history
"Balance" — you migrate only monetary totals
"Master" — all transaction data derives from master data
"Current" — you migrate only the current financial year
items.explain:
**Open items, open orders, open contracts, open internal orders…**

$$\textbf{migrate} = \textbf{the state the business is in}, \text{ not } \textbf{the story of how it got there}$$

A delivered and paid PO affects nothing going forward; **an open PO must move**, because goods will still arrive against it.

**"Material in Transit — High Seas, On Port"** is the vivid case: owned, payable, on a ship, on nobody's shelf. **Miss it and both stock and payables are wrong on day one.**

items.q: Which are component plans of an **ERP project plan**? *(select all that apply)*
options: Activity, Deliverables and Milestone plan
Resource plan
Training, Testing and Data Migration plans
Marketing plan
items.explain:
Six in all — the three above plus the **Change Management Plan**.

**Five of the six are named after the things that most often go wrong:** *lack of planning* (39% of failures), *inadequate co-ordination of resources* (26%), *no quality control* (34%), *clean data*, and *inadequate change management*.

**"Resource Plan is derived from Project Plan"** — getting that direction backwards is how *aggressive time frame* becomes an unachievable schedule.

items.q: The **Project Charter** is a major deliverable of which phase, and where is it presented?
options: Project Preparation — presented at the Kick Off Meeting
Business Blueprint — presented at the blueprint sign-off
Realization — presented at the go-live audit
Final Preparation — presented at cutover planning
items.explain:
**Project Preparation → Kick Off Meeting.**

The charter fixes **why** (overview, business case, benefits), **what** (scope, deliverables, goals), **who decides** (stakeholders, organisation and roles), **how** (strategy, plan, standards), and **what could go wrong** (assumptions, constraints, risk assessment).

**"Assumptions and Constraints" carries the most weight in practice** — writing them down converts a later argument into a documented fact.

items.q: Three of the four stated **kick-off meeting goals** are change management rather than project management. Which is the odd one out?
options: Explain the high level project plan, implementation strategy, timeline, goals and deliverables
Introduce project team members and explain their roles
Outline key Organizational Change Management goals and objectives
Create excitement about the project
items.explain:
**Only the plan explanation is project management.** The kick-off is announced to *"the whole organization"* — most of that audience will never touch the plan. **What they need is to know this is happening, that leadership is behind it, and who to talk to.**

⚠️ **"Create excitement" is a real objective, not decoration.** Whether people arrive at a disruptive change curious or resentful is substantially set on day one — and **poor communication is the 57% failure cause.**

items.q: The four **risk impact levels**, from least to most severe, are
options: Negligible → Marginal → Critical → Catastrophic
Low → Medium → High → Severe
Minor → Moderate → Major → Total
items.explain:
**Negligible** *(minor inconvenience)* → **Marginal** *(degradation of secondary mission)* → **Critical** *(serious threat to primary objective)* → **Catastrophic** *(failure of primary mission)*.

**The instruction attached is where the value is:** *"identify all **critical and catastrophic** threats… and deal with them proactively"* — you are explicitly told **not** to actively mitigate the lower two.

*(P1–P4 is the **SLA severity** scale, not the risk impact scale.)*

items.q: The deck's risk taxonomy has three nested tiers. Which risks belong to the **ERP-specific** tier? *(select all that apply)*
options: Inadequate business process reengineering
Inadequate change management
Inadequate legacy system management
Attrition
items.explain:
**Attrition is in the *every project* tier**, alongside low user involvement, poor team skills, low top management support, poor monitoring, ineffective PM techniques, scarcity of resources and changing external environment.

$$\textbf{every project} \subset \textbf{technology project} \subset \textbf{ERP project}$$

**An ERP project carries all twenty-two risks** — which is why they fail more often. *(This whole taxonomy exists **only as an image**; the slide has no text.)*

items.q: Why are **probability** and **impact** separate steps in the five-step risk approach?
options: Because risk exposure is roughly probability × impact, and neither factor alone tells you what to do
Because they are assessed by different teams
Because impact is objective and probability is subjective
Because probability determines the budget and impact determines the schedule
items.explain:
$$\textbf{risk exposure} \approx \textbf{probability} \times \textbf{impact}$$

**A catastrophic risk that is nearly impossible and a marginal risk that is certain need completely different responses.**

The five steps: **find → assess probability → analyze impact → prioritize → mitigate the top risks.** Note step 5 says *"for **top** risk elements"*, not all. **Same algorithm as MRP's exception messages and ABC-driven cycle counting.**

items.q: Which fundamental of requirements management prevents arguments at UAT?
options: "Requirement should be verifiable"
"Granularity depends on the organization"
"Prioritization of requirements is important"
"Requirements mean different things to different people"
items.explain:
**A requirement you cannot test cannot be accepted or rejected** — so it will be argued about at UAT, when it is most expensive.

| Not verifiable | Verifiable |
|---|---|
| *"the system must be user friendly"* | *"a GR must be postable in under 6 keystrokes"* |

**Same discipline as milestones** — *"to-be design completed"* rather than *"blueprinting going well."* **State it so its truth is checkable.**

items.q: Which are the **five core team responsibilities**? *(select all that apply)*
options: Provide business inputs during TO-BE process design
Validate data before loading into the new system
Train the end users, using Train the Trainer
Negotiate the licence contract with the package vendor
items.explain:
Plus **configuring the system** and **testing**. Contract negotiation belongs to the **selection committee**, not the core team.

**Each responsibility exists because only the business side can do it** — only they know a genuine duplicate from two real customers, and only they know what a correct test result looks like.

⚠️ ***"For projects to succeed the core team need to be full time"*** is the success factor most often violated — and *"ERP core team do not have the right resource"* is the corresponding failure.

items.q: Three roles appear in the project structure **"both from consulting and core team side"**. Which are they?
options: Project Manager, Module Lead, Module Team Member
Project Sponsor, Steering Committee, Process Owner
Integration Manager, Data Manager, Training Manager
Industry SME, Change Manager, Technical Lead
items.explain:
**The whole delivery spine is mirrored** — every level has someone who knows the package paired with someone who knows the business.

Option C are the **four cross-cutting roles** *(with Change Manager)* — they exist because integration, data, training and change **span every module**, and anything spanning modules is nobody's job unless someone owns it. **Each corresponds to a sub-plan of the project plan.**

**The Process Owner is explicitly "from the business side"** — they own a *process*, not a module, and they own the benefits afterwards.

items.q: What is the **most cited reason** for ERP implementation project failure, and at what percentage?
options: Poor communication between relevant parties — 57%
Lack of planning of scheduling, resources and activities — 39%
Costs getting out of hand — 20%
No quality control — 34%
items.explain:
**57%** — nearly half again the second place, and the deck notes that *"mismanagement of progress" (17%) **overlaps with poor communication***, so the true figure is higher.

**The number one cause of ERP failure is not technical.**

And the top five — communication, planning, quality control, milestones, coordination — are all **generic project-management failures**, i.e. exactly the *"risk associated with every project"* tier.

items.q: The deck annotates one failure reason as *"a symptom not a cause."* Which one, and why does it matter?
options: Costs getting out of hand — treating it as the problem leads to cutting testing and training, which worsens the actual causes
Poor communication — it is really a symptom of poor management
Milestones not being set — it is a symptom of poor planning
Supplier under-resourced — it is a symptom of poor partner selection
items.explain:
**Costs do not rise spontaneously** — they rise because scope changed, the schedule slipped, or rework was needed.

⚠️ **Treating the cost overrun as the problem leads to the wrong remedy.** Cutting testing and training reduces spend while making the underlying causes worse.

That is a genuinely sophisticated annotation and worth repeating in an answer.

items.q: Which ERP failure ended in **bankruptcy**, and what was the stated cause?
options: FoxMeyer Drug Co., 1998 — could not handle the huge volume of transactions and had integration problems
Hershey, 1999 — bugs in SAP R/3 implemented by IBM
W. L. Gore, 1997 — Deloitte & Touche not experts
Cleveland State University — full of bugs, extra hardware
items.explain:
**FoxMeyer / SAP America / Anderson Consulting — bankruptcy 1998.**

A drug distributor's entire business *is* high-volume transaction processing, so a system that cannot process the volume is **not a degraded system, it is no system.** In the risk vocabulary: **catastrophic — failure of primary mission.**

⚠️ **All four cases name a Tier 1 package and a Tier 1 or 2 firm.** Choosing famous names is not a defence.

items.q: In the change cycle, a change moves through which three environments?
options: Development → Quality/Test → Production, with an approval gate before each transport
Sandbox → Development → Production, with one approval
Development → Production → Archive
Test → Development → Production, with no formal gates
items.explain:
**The word the deck uses is "transported", and it is precise:** the same object is **moved forward**, so what was tested is exactly what goes live. **Re-doing a change in production is the failure this design prevents.**

⚠️ **Step 4 is placed *before* the final transport:** *"all documents (process and config docs) are updated with the change."* **Documentation is a precondition for going live, not a follow-up task.**

items.q: Why does the deck say cutover planning **needs to be a senior management decision**?
options: Because typically every department believes their transactions are the most critical
Because only senior management can authorise the budget
Because the go-live date affects the financial year-end
Because consultants are not permitted to decide cutover timing
items.explain:
**Ask each department and all of them will say they cannot stop.** Somebody with authority over all of them has to rank transaction criticality.

The deck's own examples are precise: **customer ordering and invoicing lose revenue if stopped**; **maintenance orders and new purchase contracts can be deferred a week.**

**Hershey's 1999 go-live near its peak season is the counter-example that made this famous.**

items.q: The deck says *"it's OK to have such issues"* at go-live. Under what two conditions?
options: No critical issues pending, and a detailed list with an agreed time frame and named owners
Fewer than ten issues, and vendor sign-off
All issues logged in the risk register, and steering committee approval
Issues resolved within the hyper-care period, whatever their severity
items.explain:
$$\textbf{go-live criterion} = \textbf{zero critical open items} + \textbf{a dated closure plan for the rest}$$

**Waiting for zero open issues means never going live.** But **an undocumented open issue is not an open issue — it is a defect that has been forgotten.**

**And note what the go-live audit checks: five of its seven items are *readiness*, not correctness** — training, UAT signoff, data migration, **support help desk**, period-end procedures.

items.q: In an SLA, what is the difference between **response time** and **solution time**?
options: Response time is how fast they get back to you; solution time is the maximum period allowed to actually fix the problem
Response time applies to P1 issues; solution time to P3 and P4
Response time is measured in hours; solution time in business days
They are the same measure under two names
items.explain:
**This is where SLAs are gamed.** *"We called you back within 15 minutes"* satisfies **response time** while the problem remains unsolved for a week.

⚠️ **A support contract with a response-time SLA and no solution-time SLA is much weaker than it looks.**

The other parameters: **service window** (support hours), **downtime** (breakdowns per year), **availability** (% uptime). **P1/P2 get 24×7 on call; P3/P4 wait for the next business day**, and **Service Level Reports (SLR)** check adherence monthly.
